verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Kakinada rice millers with verified paddy tie-ups and export order books; avoid traders riding the price spike on borrowed stock.
title: Kakinada Rice Milling & Export: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A Kakinada mill buys paddy at harvest, dries and mills it, and sells parboiled or white rice either to the state procurement system or FOB Kakinada to West African and other buyers. Cash is made on the milling margin and on the spread between paddy cost and rice price, not on volume alone. **The whole cycle is a working-capital cycle: paddy must be bought in a 6-8 week window and held as rice until it ships.** Capex is modest (mill, dryer, boiler, husk power); the balance sheet risk sits in inventory and receivables, not plant. So when a proposal lands, check paddy procurement funding and stock holding period first, not the mill's book value.

## What has changed now
Cyclone Arnab damaged more than 70 thsd ha of rice crops and over 10 thsd ha of horticulture in Andhra Pradesh, and local millers expect harvest delayed by at least 15 days [1]. Indian 5% broken parboiled rice was $375/t FOB Kakinada on 29 October, up $4/t week-on-week, with traders expecting more [1]. **Rising prices flatter a miller's P&L while hiding the fact that his paddy is not yet in the yard.** West African demand is described as subdued [1], so the price rise is supply-led, not demand-led. Separately, the Kakinada joint collector has warned millers against violating procurement norms [2], and port disruption at Kakinada and Vizag was reported in July [3]. AP GST collections are -0.2% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D] — a local stress signal — while AP electricity demand is +18.1% vs India +9.5% [D].

## Where the growth is
Peer results show the money is in branded and integrated players: KRBL posted its strongest-ever quarterly profitability with PAT of Rs. 261 crores and EBITDA margin of 23.8%, up from 13.9% [7], and Amir Chand Jagdish Kumar reported net profit up 94% to ₹366.27 million on revenue up 55% to ₹6,646.74 million [6]. **Pursue millers with their own brand, captive husk power and a repeat export buyer list; avoid pure paddy traders and mills whose only customer is a single West African buyer.** ICRA expects basmati revenue growth of 6-8% in FY2026 on export pick-up [8] — note this rating report is undated and should be treated as old.

## How to grow safely
Structure against stock, not against hope: **hypothecate paddy and rice with a stock-and-receivable statement every month, and set the drawing power on the lower of book stock and insured stock.** Take monthly stock statements, monthly export realisation statements, and quarterly GST returns. Where the borrower sells to state procurement, take the procurement order and release limit against allotment, not against mill capacity. Ask for the paddy arrival register each fortnight; if arrivals are behind the 15-day delay [1], ask whether the borrower is buying at the top of the price curve.

## Early-warning signs
- **Stock ageing beyond the normal holding period** — if rice sits unsold past the shipment cycle, cut limit and ask for the buyer contract.
- **Receivable days stretching from a single West African buyer** — if one buyer crosses a third of sales, ask for credit insurance or LC confirmation.
- **Procurement norm notices** [2] — any show-cause from the joint collector means stop fresh disbursement until resolved.
- **Port disruption recurrence** [3] — if Kakinada/Vizag shipments stall, extend the drawing-power review to weekly.
- **AP GST trend staying negative** [D] — if the borrower's own GST turnover falls two quarters running, reprice or exit.

arrivals behind 15-day delay [1] -> verify purchase price vs current market
two quarters of falling turnover -> reprice or exit
